builder_before.title: The lesson opens on a hand held in front of a torch and asks where the dark patch lands before anything is explained. It then builds the idea that light travels in straight lines from the torch, so the opaque hand stops the light that would have reached the wall and leaves an unlit region — a shadow — behind the hand, on the far side from the torch. Learners compare that case against a near-miss where the hand is moved to the side of the beam, confront the belief that the shadow is something the hand sends out, and close by explaining where the shadow falls and in which direction it would move for a new object.

nodes.text: A Torch, a Hand and a Wall

Picture a torch switched on and standing on a table, pointed at a plain wall. A hand is held up between the torch and the wall, partway along the beam. On the wall you can see a bright patch of light, and within it a dark patch shaped like the hand that is being held up. Take a moment to look at the two patches: one bright, one dark, and note where each one sits. Before anything is explained, decide for yourself: where is the dark patch — on the same side of the hand as the torch, or on the far side, and what makes you think so?

nodes.body: A torch shines on a wall. A hand is held in the space between the torch and the wall. On the wall you can see a bright patch of light and, alongside it, a dark patch shaped like the hand. Before you read any explanation, decide: where on the wall is the dark patch relative to the hand, and where do you think it will land if the hand is moved a little? Commit to your answer now and be ready to check it against the explanation that follows.
nodes.title: Pause and predict

nodes.text: Light from the torch travels outward in straight lines. The opaque hand sits in the path of those lines, so the light that would have reached one region of the wall never gets there. That region on the wall receives no light and looks dark, and this unlit region is the shadow. A shadow is not something the hand gives off or sends out; it is the place the light cannot reach because the hand is in the way. The shadow appears on the side of the hand away from the torch, because light can only be blocked downstream of its source. [P06C-BUILDER-EDIT-20260913B]

nodes.body: The torch sends light out in straight lines. The opaque hand sits in the path of those lines, so the light that would have reached one region of the wall never gets there. That region receives no light and looks dark — the shadow is simply the place the light cannot reach because the hand is in the way. Because light can only be blocked downstream of its source, the shadow falls on the side of the hand away from the torch. The hand does not give off or send out a shadow.
nodes.title: A shadow is not something the hand sends out

nodes.alt: A torch on the left shines light toward a wall on the right. Straight rays leave the torch; the central rays strike an opaque hand held in the middle of the beam and stop there, while rays passing above and below the hand continue in straight lines to the wall. On the wall beyond the hand, on the far side from the torch, is a dark hand-shaped region surrounded by lit wall.
nodes.caption: Light from the torch travels in straight lines across the gap. Where the rays meet the opaque hand, the light is stopped; rays passing beside the hand continue to the wall. The unlit region on the wall sits beyond the hand, on the far side from the torch, and its outline matches the hand's shape.

nodes.text: Follow the light rather than the hand. Light leaves the torch and travels in straight lines, so the rays spread outwards at fixed angles. Where the opaque hand stands in the beam, those rays meet the hand and stop — no light gets past it at that point. The rays that pass beside the hand are untouched, so they carry on in their straight lines until they reach the wall. Look at the wall immediately beyond the hand: the region that no ray could reach is left unlit, and that unlit region is the shadow. Its shape matches the outline of the hand standing in the beam, because each part of the hand removes exactly the rays behind it. Notice also where the dark region sits — not beside the hand and not around the torch, but on the far side of the hand from the light source, along the direction the light was travelling: from the torch, past the gap beside the hand, to the wall.
Comparing Two Arrangements: Hand in the Beam and Hand Out of the Beam

Directly between the torch and the wall
A dark hand-shaped patch on the wall beyond the hand
Torch, hand and wall, hand moved aside
Out of the beam, still in the room
No dark hand-shaped patch on the wall
nodes.caption: Two arrangements with the same torch, hand and wall. The wall shows a dark hand-shaped patch only when the hand blocks the light's straight-line path to the wall.

nodes.body: The hand is still in the room in both arrangements, and the torch is unchanged in both. Yet only one wall shows a hand-shaped dark patch. Ask yourself: what is the hand doing in the first arrangement that it is not doing in the second? A shadow is not something an object gives off. It only appears where the object stands in the light's path and stops the light that would otherwise reach the wall. If the hand is moved out of that path, nothing is blocked, and no shadow appears on the wall.
nodes.title: No blocking, no shadow

nodes.text: It is easy to feel that the shadow is something the hand gives off — that the hand sends out its own dark patch, like a puff of smoke. Before reading on, decide what that belief predicts. If the hand produced its own shadow, the dark patch should appear wherever the hand is placed, and it should sit on the lit side of the hand, facing the torch. Now compare that with what actually happens. When the hand is moved to the side of the beam, out of the torch's light, no shadow lands on the wall at all — even though the hand is still there, and still just as solid. When the hand is held between the torch and the wall, the dark region does not sit on the hand's lit side; it falls on the far side, away from the torch. The emit-a-shadow belief fails both tests: it predicts a shadow when there is none, and it predicts the wrong side when a shadow is there. The blocking account passes both. Light travels in straight lines from the torch, the opaque hand stops the light that would have reached the wall, and the region where that light fails to arrive is unlit. So a shadow is an absence of light on the far side of an opaque object — not something the hand emits.

nodes.body:
Before checking the next arrangement, commit to a prediction. If the shadow were something the hand gives off or sends out, where would the dark patch appear? It would appear wherever the hand was placed, and it would sit on the lit side of the hand, facing the torch.

Now test that idea. Move the hand to the side, out of the beam: the hand is still there, but no shadow appears on the wall. Put the hand back in the beam: the dark region sits on the side of the hand away from the torch. The emit-a-shadow belief predicts the wrong presence and the wrong side. The blocking account predicts both correctly: the shadow is an absence of light on the far side of the object, not something the hand emits.
nodes.title: Does the hand send out its own shadow?

nodes.text: Where does the shadow fall now?

The torch, the hand and the wall stay in the same arrangement as before, but the hand is now held at a new position in front of the torch, with the wall left where it is. The torch is still the light source. Before you can say where the dark hand-shaped patch lands, trace what the light does: rays leave the torch and travel in straight lines to the wall unless something stops them. The opaque hand stands in the way, so the light that would have reached the wall is blocked by it. As a result, the wall behind the hand receives no light from the torch, and the dark patch falls on the far side of the hand from the torch — never between the torch and the hand. From there, describe the direction it moves relative to the light source: if the hand is moved towards the torch, the patch shifts; if the hand is moved away from the torch, the patch shifts in the opposite direction along the same line. Explain, using the straight-line blocking account, where the patch now falls and which way it moves when the hand's position changes, rather than simply saying that a shadow is formed.

sections.title: Give the learner a reason to care and a concrete situation to hold.
Build the idea itself. State it, ground it, make it usable.

feedback.incorrect: Look again at the two arrangements. The hand does not make darkness on its own, and the wall does not decide. A shadow appears only when the opaque hand blocks light that is travelling in a straight line from the torch.

options.text: The hand gives out its own shadow, which lands on the wall.
options.explanation: This treats the shadow as something sent out by the hand, but light is blocked by the opaque hand rather than shadow being emitted.

options.text: The opaque hand blocks light, so an unlit region forms on the far side.
options.explanation: Light travels in straight lines from the torch; the opaque hand stops it, creating a shadow on the side away from the light source.

options.text: The shadow forms on the lit side of the hand, facing the torch.
options.explanation: This reverses the position: the shadow appears on the side opposite the light source, not on the lit side facing the torch.

options.text: The wall reflects the torchlight back onto the hand as a dark patch.
options.explanation: Reflection is not what makes the shadow; the shadow is the absence of light where the opaque hand has blocked it.

contract.prompt: A torch shines on a hand, and a dark shadow appears on the wall behind it. What causes the shadow?

feedback.correct: Yes. Light travels in straight lines from the torch, and the opaque hand blocks it, leaving an unlit shadow on the wall on the far side of the hand.

contract.prompt: A hand blocks the light from a torch, making a hand-shaped shadow on the wall. If the hand is moved to a new position in front of the torch while the wall stays where it is, where does the dark hand-shaped patch fall, and how does its position change relative to the light source?

feedback.correct: Yes. The hand is opaque, so it blocks the straight-line light from the torch. The unlit region forms on the far side, opposite the torch, so as the hand moves relative to the light the shadow shifts accordingly.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at the straight-line path of light from the torch. The hand is opaque and stops the light, so the unlit patch appears on the side of the hand opposite the torch, not between the hand and the torch, on the hand, or beside the torch.

document.title: The lesson opens on a hand held in front of a torch and asks where the dark patch lands before anything is explained. It then builds the idea that light travels in straight lines from the torch, so the opaque hand stops the light that would have reached the wall and leaves an unlit region — a shadow — behind the hand, on the far side from the torch. Learners compare that case against a near-miss where the hand is moved to the side of the beam, confront the belief that the shadow is something the hand sends out, and close by explaining where the shadow falls and in which direction it would move for a new object.

sections.title: Give the learner a reason to care and a concrete situation to hold.
Build the idea itself. State it, ground it, make it usable.
sections.transition: The learner has committed to where the dark patch falls; this section now says why it must fall there.

sections.title: Put a case and a near-miss side by side. The learner must see the boundary of the idea, not just the idea.
sections.transition: The learner now has the torch–hand–wall account; this section tests its edge by changing one condition — whether the hand is in the beam at all.

sections.title: The shared diagnostic. Identical across every variant. Written from the card only, never from the prose above it.
sections.transition: The learner has seen the mechanism and its boundary; this section checks whether the objective has landed on the same setup with the object moved.
